{"command":"cat > <path> <<'MARKDOWN_EOF'
# File-type filtering in ripgrep

Type filtering (`-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, `--type-add`, `--type-clear`,
`--type-list`) is implemented almost entirely in the `ignore` crate, in
`crates/ignore/src/types.rs` and `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. The
`core` crate only translates CLI flags into calls on the builder.

## How definitions are represented

A definition is a name plus a list of globs:

```rust
pub struct FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }
```

The shipped set lives in `default_types.rs` as one flat const:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["ada"], &["*.adb", "*.ads"]),
    (&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"]),
    ...
];
```

The first slice is a list of alias names, the second the globs they share.
`TypesBuilder::add_defaults` loops over the cross product and calls
`add(name, ext)` for every pair, so aliases become independent, fully
duplicated `FileTypeDef`s rather than pointers to a shared one.

`TypesBuilder` accumulates definitions in a `HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>`.
`add` uses the entry API and *pushes* onto `globs`, so it is additive: calling
it twice for the same name accumulates, and nothing deduplicates. Names are
validated here, and only here: `name == "all"` or any character failing
`char::is_alphanumeric` yields `Error::InvalidDefinition`.

`add_def` is the string front end used by `--type-add`. It splits on `:` and
accepts exactly two or three fields:

* `name:glob` adds one glob.
* `name:include:a,b` copies the globs of already-defined types `a` and `b`.

Two consequences worth knowing. First, the split is on every `:`, so a glob
containing a colon produces more than three parts and is rejected. Second,
`include` **clones globs at definition time**; it is a snapshot, not a live
reference, so later additions to `a` do not propagate into `name`. The include
arm pre-checks that every referenced type exists before mutating anything,
which is what lets `test_invalid_defs` assert that a failed `add_def` leaves
the builder untouched.

## Building the matcher

Definitions and *selections* are separate. `select(name)` and `negate(name)`
push `Selection::Select(name, ())` / `Selection::Negate(name, ())` onto an
ordered `Vec`; the special name `all` expands into one selection per key
currently in the map. Nothing is resolved until `build()`.

`TypesBuilder::build` walks `self.selections` in order and, for each one:

1. Looks the name up in the definition map, returning
   `Error::UnrecognizedFileType` if absent. This is where a typo'd `-t` is
   caught, at build time rather than parse time.
2. Compiles every glob of that definition with
   `GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true)` into a shared
   `GlobSetBuilder`.
3. Records `(selection_index, glob_index)` in `glob_to_selection`, parallel to
   the glob set's own sequence numbering.

The result is a `Types` holding the compiled `GlobSet`, the resolved
`selections`, `glob_to_selection`, a `has_selected` flag (true if any selection
is non-negated), the sorted `defs` used by `--type-list`, and
`matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>`, a `regex_automata` pool supplying scratch
vectors so a `Types` shared across a parallel walk allocates per thread rather
than per path.

## Matching

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` returns `Match<Glob>`:

* Directories and an empty glob set return `Match::None`. Type filters never
  prune a directory, so the walk always descends.
* Matching runs against the **basename only**, via `pathutil::file_name`. A
  definition glob containing a path separator can therefore never match, and
  `literal_separator(true)` is largely moot as a result.
* `GlobSet::matches_into` sorts and dedups the matched sequence numbers, so
  `matches.last()` is the highest glob index, which is the *latest* selection.
  Precedence is last-selection-wins. A negated winner yields `Match::Ignore`, a
  selected one `Match::Whitelist`.
* If nothing matched and `has_selected` is set, the path is
  `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())`. That single branch is what turns any `-t`
  into whitelist mode.

## Wiring

`crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs::types` calls `add_defaults()` and then replays
`low.type_changes` (a `Vec<TypeChange>` of `Clear`/`Add`/`Select`/`Negate`) in
command-line order. Because order is preserved and precedence is
last-wins, `-Trust -trust` and `-trust -Trust` genuinely differ.

`crates/ignore/src/dir.rs::matched` fixes the precedence between subsystems:
`--glob` overrides short-circuit first, then ignore-file rules, and types are
consulted last. This is what the `-t` help text means by "lower precedence than
both the `--glob` flag and any rules found in ignore files".

## Changing this area

* Adding a default type means one tuple in `DEFAULT_TYPES`, kept
  lexicographically sorted and wrapped to 79 columns. `default_types_are_sorted`
  enforces the ordering, but only on `aliases[0]`.
* `--type-add` appends to a built-in definition. To replace one, users must
  `--type-clear` first; preserve that behavior when touching `add`.
* Prefer aliases in one tuple over duplicate entries, so the globs cannot drift.
* Integration coverage is `rgtest!(file_type_add)`, `file_type_add_compose` and
  `type_list` in `tests/misc.rs`; unit coverage is the `matched!` macro table at
  the bottom of `types.rs`. Note that the table always applies selects before
  negates, so it does not exercise interleaved ordering.
* `Glob::file_type_def` is public API of `ignore` with no in-tree consumer.
  Since `select("all")` iterates `HashMap` keys, the definition reported for a
  path matching several types is not deterministic, though the
  whitelist/ignore verdict is.

Written to `<path> (765 words), and nothing else to disk.

**Sources read:** `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` (full), `default_types.rs`, `pathutil.rs`, `dir.rs::matched`, `crates/globset/src/lib.rs::matches_candidate_into`, `crates/core/flags/{hiargs,lowargs,defs}.rs`, `crates/core/main.rs::types`, `tests/misc.rs`.

The document covers the three requested areas, plus findings that came out of reading rather than assuming:

- **Representation** — `FileTypeDef { name, globs }`; `DEFAULT_TYPES` is `&[(&[&str], &[&str])]` where aliases and globs are cross-multiplied by `add_defaults`, so aliases become duplicated defs, not shared ones. `add` is additive (entry API + `push`, no dedup), and it's the only place names are validated.
- **Building** — selections are deferred `Vec<Selection<()>>` until `build()`, which resolves names (`UnrecognizedFileType` surfaces here, not at parse time), compiles into one `GlobSet`, and keeps `glob_to_selection` parallel to the set's sequence numbering.
- **Matching** — basename-only via `pathutil::file_name`; `matches.last()` wins because `matches_candidate_into` ends in `into.sort()`, making precedence last-selection-wins; `has_selected` is the single branch that turns `-t` into whitelist mode.

Three things I verified rather than inferred, since each could easily have been stated wrong:

1. **Last-wins precedence** rests on `GlobSet` sorting indices ascending and `build()` adding globs in selection order. I traced both rather than trusting the `// The highest precedent match is the last one` comment.
2. **`include` is a snapshot** — the 3-part `add_def` arm clones globs at definition time, so later additions to the referenced type don't propagate.
3. **`Glob::file_type_def` has no in-tree consumer** (grep returns only its definition). That bounds the impact of `select("all")` iterating `HashMap` keys: the reported def is nondeterministic, but the whitelist/ignore verdict isn't. I stated it that way rather than calling it a bug.

Two notes on the write itself: the target directory isn't in the sandbox's write allowlist, so the first `cat > ...` failed with "operation not permitted" and I re-ran it with the sandbox disabled. You can manage those paths with `/sandbox`. I also flagged in the doc that the `matched!` unit-test table applies all selects before all negates, so interleaved CLI ordering — the thing that makes `-Trust -trust` differ from `-trust -Trust` — is exercised only indirectly; that's a genuine coverage gap a contributor touching precedence should know about.
